next_steps: Maya to send benchmark template and sample prompts
Customer to provide 72h traffic trace + sample payloads
Schedule benchmark run for next Tue/Thu window
Share SOC2 + network diagram with Rajiv
action_items: Maya - send benchmark template and pricing estimate by 2027-03-18
Emily - upload 72h traffic trace and sample prompts to shared folder by 2027-03-19

summary: POC scoping call focused on workload characterization and traffic modeling for MistralPay's customer support assistant. Agreed to run a 72h benchmark with sample prompts. Success criteria: 95th pctl latency < 250ms on 512-token outputs, semantic fidelity within current baseline, and cost target <$0.05 per 1k output tokens. Initial target traffic ~25 QPS steady with bursts to 100 QPS; average input tokens ~40, avg output ~120. Next: Redwood to send benchmark template and recommended config; customer to upload traces.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-16 15:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Emily Chen (MistralPay Head of ML), Rajiv Kapoor (Platform), Lisa Gomez (CTO), Omar Siddiqui (SRE)

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm maya from redwood inference. quick roll call?
[00:10] Emily: hi emily here, thanks for setting this up.
[00:12] Rajiv: rajiv on platform.
[00:14] Lisa: lisa, cto.
[00:15] Omar: omar, sre.
[00:17] Carlos: carlos here, solutions eng, good to meet you all.

[00:22] Maya: goal for today is to scope the poc for workload and traffic modeling — we want to lock success criteria, get QPS/concurrency numbers, token distributions and then agree on a benchmark plan and timeline.

[00:35] Emily: high level, we want to replace our current rule-based email triage w/ a llm assistant. Currently about 2 million messages/month, peak concurrent ~250 active sessions but only a subset hitting the assistant. We estimate 25 qps steady for the assistant, spikes to 80-120 during promos.

[01:05] Rajiv: just to add, our critical constraint is latency during live chat — business expects snappy responses (<300ms ideally) and throughput for batched nightly categorization also matters.

[01:25] Carlos: okay great; maya, are you able to speak to what redwood typically sees for this class of workload and which models make sense?

[01:32] Maya: yeah for the POC we usually recommend starting with a 13B-ish open model quantized (llama-2-13b or equivalent) on redwood dedicated for predictable throughput; hosted api is possible but dedicated gives clearer perf numbers for benchmarks. we can also run a quick hosted baseline.

[01:50] Emily: on quality we need parity with our in-house fine-tuned model — it's not perfect but passes our intent classification at 92% f1. success criteria should include qualitative evals (sample prompt set) plus throughput and latency.

[02:10] Carlos: makes sense — so success criteria we propose: (1) 95th percentile latency < 250ms for typical chat requests (~512 tokens total), (2) quality within 5% relative f1 on the eval set, (3) unit cost under your target — what is that, emily?

[02:30] Emily: we'd like to keep model runtime cost under $0.05 per 1k output tokens as a target for production, but understand poc might be higher.

[02:42] Lisa: timeline question — how long for the POC to get meaningful numbers? two to four weeks?

[02:50] Jordan: realistically, once we have traces and sample prompts, we can configure and run a 72-hour benchmark within 7-10 days, then analyze. end-to-end POC to a decision could be 3-6 weeks depending on approvals.

[03:10] Rajiv: ok, we'll need a weekend test window too since our peak happens on weekends — also we have strict network controls and a private subnet where production lives.

[03:25] Maya: noted — we support private deployments (VPC) and can run on your VPC or Redwood private control plane; we'll include network diagram in the security pack.

[03:40] Omar: small point — we use KMS for keys and need audit logs retained 1 year. SOC2 is mandatory.

[03:48] Carlos: we have SOC2 docs, and support KMS/HSM integrations and audit log export. we'll share that with you.

[04:00] Maya: let's dig into traffic characterization — you said 2M messages/month; what's the breakdown of message lengths and typical reply size?

[04:12] Emily: on input tokens most messages are very short: ~60% under 64 tokens, 30% between 64-256, and 10% over 256 (edge cases). output average is around 120 tokens but varies; occasionally we generate longer threaded replies up to 512 tokens for summaries.

[04:38] Carlos: for modeling we'll need percentile distributions. for the poc we usually model avg input 40 tokens, avg output 120 tokens, with p95 output ~320 tokens to be safe.

[04:50] Maya: qps targets again? you mentioned 25 steady; does that correspond to concurrent sessions -- what's your concurrency expectation?

[04:58] Rajiv: we'd estimate steady concurrency ~30-40 workers (chat sessions), each sending a request roughly every 2-3 minutes. bursts hit 100 qps for a 10-20 minute window.

[05:15] Carlos: great — so for capacity planning we should model: steady 25 qps, burst 100 qps, concurrency up to 40. That maps to req/sec and token/sec numbers.

[05:30] Jordan: quick note on caching — many chats share the same prefixes (greetings, context) so prefix/KV caching can reduce repeated compute. if 20-30% of calls benefit from cache we can reduce token compute.

[05:45] Emily: can you explain how caching works with ongoing sessions? we use context windows with KV cache in production right now — curious about eviction and staleness.

[05:55] Carlos: sure — kv cache stores key/value activations for prior tokens; for streaming chat we keep session-level KV lasting the conversation length and evict by LRU after a threshold. for POC we can instrument cache hit rates and show token savings.

[06:10] Maya: also batching — for non-interactive flows (nightly categorization) we can run large batch jobs which amortize cost per token. for live chat we use small batching to maintain latency.

[06:25] Rajiv: any rules of thumb for tokens per GPU? we run on A100ish in infra — curious what peak throughput looks like.

[06:33] Carlos: numbers vary by model and quantization. as an example, a quantized 13B on our runtime can do ~600-900 tokens/sec per GPU in optimized path for generation workloads; that translates to many concurrent short chats. longer outputs push GPU time. we'll include model-specific perf profiles in the benchmark template.

[06:55] Lisa: and fallback behavior? if dedicated capacity is saturated what happens?

[07:00] Maya: we have routing policies — fall back to hosted or a cheaper model variant; can do canary rollouts and A/B. for critical flows we recommend multi-tier routing: priority goes to dedicated pool, then capacity tier, then model variant.

[07:18] Emily: for the benchmark we want to see latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), token throughput, cost breakdown (compute vs infra), and quality metrics (f1 on intents + a few human-eval samples).

[07:32] Carlos: agreed. we'll also capture per-route traces and per-token latency so you can see where time is spent (decode vs kernel launch vs io).

[07:45] Jordan: can we capture a sample of failed requests or rate limited responses? helpful for SRE.

[07:50] Omar: yes please include error logs and retry behavior. we run strict retry policies at network layer.

[08:00] Maya: timeline and milestones — propose: (1) by 2027-03-18 we send benchmark template + prompts, (2) by 2027-03-19 customer uploads 72h trace, (3) 2027-03-22 we run initial hosted baseline, (4) 2027-03-25 run dedicated benchmark and analyze. Decision review 2027-03-29. does that work?

[08:26] Lisa: that's aggressive but doable if approvals are fast.

[08:30] Emily: we have to get legal sign-off for network access; that may add 3-5 days.

[08:36] Maya: good call — we'll plan contingency.

[08:40] Carlos: small technical clarifications: please include sample payload schemas (headers, session id, conversation history length) and whether you plan to truncate context or send full history.

[08:55] Rajiv: we usually send the last 3 messages + metadata — full history is stored but not sent every time; sometimes we include a 1-2 sentence summary.

[09:05] Jordan: ok that helps for token modeling; please annotate how often summaries are used in sample trace.

[09:15] Emily: on metrics we also care about cold start behavior — our app scales from zero to spike quickly, so startup latency for new model workers matters.

[09:25] Carlos: we'll measure cold-start p95 as part of the benchmark and show warm vs cold performance.

[09:35] Maya: any compliance questions up front? we've mentioned SOC2, KMS, audit logs.

[09:40] Omar: also data residency — some EU customers' data must stay in eu-west region; might need region pinning for part of traffic.

[09:48] Maya: we support region routing and can pin to eu regions for specific tenant traffic; we'll note that in the SOW.

[09:55] Lisa: cost modeling — can you provide an estimate board-level: for 25 qps steady with our token distribution what is expected monthly spend? ballpark is ok.

[10:08] Carlos: rough back-of-envelope: assume avg output 120 tokens and avg input 40 tokens => 160 tokens per request. At 25 qps steady that's ~4k tokens/sec => ~345M tokens/day. Cost depends on model/cartridge; for quantized 13B on dedicated we estimate $X (we'll supply numbers in pricing sheet) but target is to be under your $0.05 per 1k output tokens. we'll give a detailed breakdown in the template.

[10:40] Emily: please include a comparison row vs our current infra cost so we can evaluate savings.

[10:48] Maya: will do.

[10:52] Jordan: operational notes — we'll capture per-route dashboards: token/sec, latency, cost/time, cache hit rate, and model version.

[11:00] Emily: any blockers from redwood side?

[11:04] Maya: none, just need the traces and prompt set, and we'll handle the rest.

[11:10] Carlos: we'll also include a recommended quantization profile and batching config for live vs batch flows.

[11:20] Lisa: ok sounds good. last q: who owns the A/B experiment if we do a progressive rollout?

[11:26] Maya: we usually set up the routing and can hand over the config to your platform team; we can run a canary with auto-fallback.

[11:35] Emily: great.

[11:40] Maya: recap of next steps and action items... (recap)

[11:47] Maya: 1) Maya send benchmark template + pricing (due 3/18). 2) Emily upload 72h trace + prompt set (due 3/19). 3) Carlos prepare config & run hosted baseline (3/22). 4) Run dedicated benchmark (3/25). 5) Review and decision 3/29.

[11:58] Lisa: thanks everyone.

[12:00] Meeting ended.

Notes: transcription has some mis-hearings; product names may be slightly off (Redwood Dedicated sometimes transcribed as Redwood Dedicate).
